title: The Lost Capital of Old Ghana

pages.text: On the first day of history class, Mr Larbi unrolled a map of West Africa and pointed far to the north-west, away from the Gulf of Guinea. “In the year 300, a powerful kingdom called Wagadu was growing here,” he said. “Traders and writers called it Ghana. That name was the title of its ruler, and it is where our country’s name comes from.”
sentences: On the first day of history class, Mr Larbi unrolled a map of West Africa and pointed far to the north-west, away from the Gulf of Guinea.
“In the year 300, a powerful kingdom called Wagadu was growing here,” he said.
“Traders and writers called it Ghana.
That name was the title of its ruler, and it is where our country’s name comes from.”
pages.alt: A teacher points to the Sahel on a map of West Africa.

pages.text: “But we are not there,” said Bintu, tracing the map. “Our Ghana is far to the south.” “Exactly,” said Mr Larbi. “The old Ghana Empire was in what is now south-east Mauritania and western Mali. In 1957, our country, then the Gold Coast, took the name Ghana at independence. Today’s mystery is simple: where, exactly, was its capital?”

pages.alt: Students look from a map of the Sahel to a map of modern Ghana.

pages.text: “We know of the old empire mostly from writers who visited or asked traders,” said Mr Larbi. “One was al-Bakri, who wrote about two towns about ten kilometres apart that were joined by houses. Another, al-Idrisi, put the royal city on a riverbank.” Gideon frowned. “Different writers, different places?”

“Different writers, different places?”
pages.alt: Old manuscripts with Arabic writing and a map beside them.

pages.text: “Most historians say the capital was probably Koumbi Saleh,” said Mr Larbi. “Its ruins lie on the edge of the Sahara. But, and this is the mystery, scholars increasingly disagree. The remains of the royal town described have not been found. Some historians suggest the capital moved over time.”

pages.alt: Ruins of stone buildings in sand under a bright sky.

pages.text: Bintu made a chart. Evidence one: writers’ descriptions, which do not always agree. Evidence two: archaeology at Koumbi Saleh, which is real, but may not be the royal town. Evidence three: oral traditions of the Soninke people, who are linked to the old empire. “So it is a puzzle with three kinds of clues,” she said. “And none is complete.”

pages.alt: A student’s chart lists three kinds of evidence and their limits.

pages.text: “How could we solve it?” asked Gideon. “More digging, in more places,” said Mr Larbi, “better dating of finds, and careful comparison of the old writings with the land. Historians sometimes disagree for decades. That is not failure. It is how knowledge grows.” Bintu wrote: Disagreement + evidence = progress.

pages.text: “Why did our country choose the name Ghana?” asked Bintu. Mr Larbi replied carefully. “In 1957 the leaders of the Gold Coast took the name of an old West African empire as their country’s name, which is why you find ‘Ghana’ on our flag, coins and certificates. I will not guess every reason. You should read what the leaders themselves said.”

pages.alt: A Ghana flag and a school certificate with the name Ghana.

pages.text: At the end, Gideon wrote a note for the class wall: The old Ghana Empire was real. Its capital is probably Koumbi Saleh, but historians still argue. Bintu added: We carry the name of a mystery. Mr Larbi nodded. “And you are the new generation who might help solve it,” he said. The end.

activities.question: Where was the old Ghana Empire located?

activities.prompt: Historians disagree about where the capital stood. What kind of evidence could help most?
options: More digging and better dating of finds

activities.question: What is the main reason the capital’s location is still debated?
options: The writings do not agree and the royal town’s remains have not been found
Nobody has heard of the empire
